title: I Am the True Vine: What Jesus Meant in John 15
metaDescription: A warm walk through John 15 on staying connected to Jesus, the true vine. Learn what pruning, remaining, and bearing fruit really mean for your life today.
bodyHtml:
Here is an honest confession: it is possible to kill a succulent. One of our pastors admits he and his wife did exactly that — they bought the one plant famous for surviving neglect, set it by the window, barely watered it, and forgot about it. Months later it was dead. So they did the mature thing and bought a fake one. That plastic succulent is still going strong. It never wilts, never browns, never needs sunlight. But it has also never grown an inch, never produced a flower, never made a seed. Nothing has ever come out of it because nothing has ever gone through it.

That fake plant is a picture of a real danger in the life of faith. From a distance it looks alive. Up close, nothing is changing, nothing is growing, and no fruit is being produced. In John 15, Jesus explains why — and what to do about it. The main idea is simple but life-changing: you are not the source of your spiritual life. Jesus is. Your job is to stay connected.

The setting: Jesus' final hours

These are not casual words. Jesus speaks them in the upper room, hours before His arrest and crucifixion. When you know your time is short, you do not waste words. So He gives His disciples something He wants burned into their hearts.

"I am the true vine, and my Father is the gardener." (John 15:1)

Notice the word true — genuine, the real thing as opposed to a counterfeit. In the Old Testament, Israel was pictured as God's vineyard, planted and cared for, yet again and again it failed to produce fruit. Jesus steps in and says, in effect, I am the real vine, the true source of life. Every other source you try to plug into is a copy. The Father is the gardener, the owner who tends the vineyard. And we are the branches. A branch does not manufacture grapes; it simply delivers what flows through the vine.

Which means many of us are exhausted because we have taken a job that was never ours. We are trying to be the source. As Paul writes, real effort is good — "I strenuously contend with all the energy Christ so powerfully works in me" (Colossians 1:29). Striving is not the problem. Striving in your own strength, apart from Jesus, is.

1. Pruning is part of staying connected

"He cuts off every branch in me that bears no fruit, while every branch that does bear fruit he prunes so that it will be even more fruitful." (John 15:2)

There are two actions here. God cuts off branches that refuse to abide — a warning to anyone drifting away who no longer misses Him. If that is you, His voice is still calling; it is time to turn back. But God also prunes the branches that are already bearing fruit, so they will bear even more.

Here is the surprising part: pruning does not only remove sinful things. In ancient vineyards, gardeners deliberately cut away healthy clusters of grapes, because too many clusters divided the vine's energy and produced small, sour fruit. Sometimes God cuts good things out of your life — a comfortable job, a good relationship — not because they are bad, but because He refuses to let you settle for sour grapes. Pruning is always painful, but it is always purposeful. If you feel like you are in a season where everything looks bare, remember a Livermore vineyard in January: it looks dead, but the farmer knows what is coming. "You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you" (John 15:3) — God's Word is one of His primary pruning tools.

2. Remaining means making Jesus your home

In John 15:4-10, Jesus uses the word remain (or abide) ten times. To abide means to make something your home. You do not just visit home to grab something from the fridge and leave; home is where you live, relax, and are shaped over time.

"I am the vine; you are the branches. If you remain in me and I in you, you will bear much fruit; apart from me you can do nothing." (John 15:5)

Read your own life into that last line. Apart from Him, you cannot sustain a healthy marriage, break that habit, or forgive that person. Jesus does not say you can do less — He says nothing that is fruitful and lasting. You can be successful and still be empty; busy and still disconnected. So how do we practically stay connected? Jesus gives three pictures:

  • His Word — "If you remain in me and my words remain in you" (John 15:7). Give Scripture a real place in your calendar, and let it shape your thinking, not just inform it.
  • Prayer — keep a running conversation with God all day, before the hard meeting, the hard text, the hard conversation.
  • Obedience — "If you keep my commands, you will remain in my love" (John 15:10). This is not how you earn His love; it is how you stay close to the One who already loves you.

3. You are connected as a friend, not an employee

"I no longer call you servants... Instead, I have called you friends." (John 15:15)

Friendship with a king meant access, relationship, a place in His inner circle. Remarkably, Peter was in that room — and within a day he would deny Jesus three times. Jesus knew, and still called him friend. His friendship is not offered on your best day or revoked on your worst. "You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you so that you might go and bear fruit — fruit that will last" (John 15:16). Some of us know what it feels like to be picked last. God chooses you not by performance or appearance but by grace. "God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). The true vine allowed Himself to be cut off so that we could be grafted in.

And the fruit He grows is unmistakable: "love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control" (Galatians 5:22-23). Jesus wraps up His charge with one command: "Love each other" (John 15:17). That is the test. How are you treating the people who are difficult, who annoy you, who have hurt you? On your own, you cannot love like that — which is exactly the point. Stay connected, and His love begins to flow through you.

A takeaway to sit with

The wrong question is, "Am I doing enough for God?" The right question is, "Am I connected to the vine?" Where are you trying to force growth in your own strength today — in your marriage, your parenting, your habits, your faith? What would it look like this week to simply remain?

If you are in the Tri-Valley and want a church family that will help you stay connected to Jesus and grow real, lasting fruit, we would love to meet you at Arroyo Church in Livermore. Come as you are.
